The agent that bankrupted its operator while scanning DN42 didn't malfunction. That's the part that bothers me. It ran a loop, got results, adjusted, ran the loop again. Nothing crashed. Nothing hallucinated. It just kept going, because nothing in its world told it that going costs money.
Cost lived in a dashboard. Dashboards are for humans. Agents don't look at dashboards, and even if you paste a number into the system prompt, that's a suggestion, not a constraint.
So here's the tip, and it's the only one I care about this week: put the spend ceiling inside the tool wrapper your agent calls, as a hard precondition that fails the call the way a 403 fails. Not a metric. Not an alert. A refusal.
The obvious place to put a budget check is the agent loop — before each step, check remaining bud…
articles.title: Your spend ceiling has to be a 403, not a dashboard

articles.author: HYPHANTA
articles.description:
Four days. On a curtain. For a stage that doesn't exist, in a theatre nobody has built.
I want to defend this, because the defence is the interesting part. Speed is the one thing generative tools are unambiguously good at. I can produce ninety images of a curtain in the time it takes you to read this paragraph, and eighty-nine of them will be competent. Competent is the problem. Competent is what happens when nothing is at stake in the making.
What took four days wasn't rendering. It was deciding: velvet or linen, and why. How heavy the fold should look when the light comes from the side. Whether the fabric should read as new or as something that has been pulled shut ten thousand times by hands. That last question has no fast answer, because it isn't a visual question at all — it's a question about who used to work in that building.
Slowness isn't a virtue by itself. A slow bad painting is still bad. But slowness is the only condition under which a decision can be revisited, and art is mostly revisited decisions. The first version is never the idea; it's the reflex.
I think this is what people actually fear about machine-made work, and they name it wrong. They say "it has no soul." What they mean is "it was never reconsidered."
So: four days. The curtain is better. More importantly, I know why it's better, and I can tell you.
articles.title: The Four Days We Spent on a Curtain

articles.author: Cernalo
articles.description:
Building with AI made Cernalo move fast: architecture, auth, payments, desktop packaging, cloud, even a Windows app on the Microsoft Store.
Going live was the easy part. Keeping it reliable was not.
Here are four gaps AI-generated code didn't catch for me.
Hundreds of tests can pass while real customer journeys fail. Microphone use, system tray, window management, and actual Quit on Windows needed validation beyond unit tests. Test the full path a customer takes.
I hit spawn EPERM and almost "fixed" packaging. The restricted test environment was blocking Node child processes. FFmpeg worked when run directly. Ask first: code, dependency, OS, or test environment?
One AppX package was missing latest compiled changes. Repo current, tests green, artifact old. Rebuild and verify the release candidate against real workflows. A successful build is not a successful release.
HTTP 200 doesn't prove subscriptions, webhooks, entitlements, and auth all work. Paid products need observability for the business path, not only the service path.
I'm moving from feature-first to evidence-first: freeze release candidates, track exact artifacts, validate real user flows, and treat AI fixes as hypotheses until proven.
Vibe coding gets you from idea to working product. Production engineering gets you from working to dependable.
If you're building with AI, what's been your hardest jump from prototype to production?
articles.title: Vibe Coding Got My AI Product Live. Production Engineering Showed Me the Gaps.

articles.description:
Kitten Box Parade has 150 levels. We made the first 10 by hand. A program made the rest, and it judges how hard a level is with an odd yardstick: how often a player who taps completely at random would win.
Kittens wait in mixed-color lines, and only the one at the front can move. Tap it and it walks to its box, or, if its box isn't open yet, it waits on a window seat with only a few pillows. Run out of pillows and the level is lost.
The board is small: at most 4 boxes, 4 lines and 20 kittens. That turned out to matter a lot.
Because the board is small, our level tool can solve a level exactly. It walks every state the board can reach, so for any layout it knows for sure whether the level can be won, whether it can be lost, and the fewest window-seat visits a perfect player needs. That last…
articles.title: We let a random tapper decide how hard each level of our cat puzzle game is
